newsitem.title: JAPAN: Chirac to visit Japan in bid to mend fences.
newsitem.headline: Chirac to visit Japan in bid to mend fences.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac's state visit to Japan next week is aimed mainly at bolstering a gradually recovering Franco-Japanese relationship, but not everyone has forgotten the row over France's South Pacific nuclear tests last year.
Tokyo's grassroots anti-nuclear activists are especially reluctant to bury the hatchet.

"The nuclear problem is not over yet," said Ichiro Murakami, a leading member of a Tokyo anti-nuclear group. "Chirac's been to Japan, several times, but it'll be the first time since he's been elected president and we intend to bring home our message," he added.
Chirac's visit will also be his first since France's nuclear tests triggered a frenzy of protest across most of the Pacific last year. He will arrive on Sunday and leave on Thursday.

The series of nuclear blasts in French Polynesia, which began on September 8, 1995, sparked public outcry and calls to boycott French products. Demonstrators camped out in front of the French embassy for days on end.
The finance minister at the time, Masayoshi Takemura, flew to Tahiti to join in his private capacity as part of a swarm of protestors from around the globe.

Murakami said his group -- aptly called the People in front of the French Embassy -- plans to rally in front of the embassy on Sunday and call on the president to visit Nagasaki and Hiroshima instead of a planned sumo tournament in Fukuoka city on the southern island of Kyushu.
"He should be visiting Hiroshima and Nagasaki, not a sumo tournament," he said.
The two cities, ground zero for the only nuclear bombs ever used in combat, are now rallying points for Japan's anti-nuclear activists.
France detonated a total of six nuclear bombs over a four month period which ended January 30.

Japanese government officials said the official trip will be aimed mainly at strengthening economic and consultative relations between the two nations. The nuclear issue will not be discussed, officials said.
On Tuesday, Japan and France are scheduled to announce a twenty point action plan accord between the two nations, officials added.
This document, which will be published following the meeting of the two heads of government, will serve as a guideline for future Franco-Japanese cooperation, they said.
One official said the meeting between Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and Chirac should "restore" bilateral relationships to where they were before the nuclear tests.
